 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (“ALJs”):

        Brushy Mountain Road Maintenance Association, Inc.; Rio Agua Investments,

 LLC; KDCB Garrett Ranch LTD; SSS Land Holdings, LLC; and BTR Burnet LP

 (together, the “Colorado River Alliance Intervenors” or “CRAI”) file this Reply Brief

 pursuant to SOAH Order No. 6 and the further orders of the ALJs and respectfully show

 the following:

 I.     INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY.

        Like the other recent 765-kV transmission line routing disputes, the intervenor

 initial briefs in this docket generally fall into four camps: (1) objections to the need of the

 project, (2) recommendations of a specific route for the Commission to approve, (3)

 oppositions to a specific route or routes, or (4) oppositions to the use of a certain link or

 set of links. Also like the other recent 765-kV cases, the intervenors who participated in

 this case are varied, comprising single families, such as the Joiners (who oppose use of

 Link E4); entire counties, such as Willamson County (which opposes Routes 295, 296,

 SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                     1
 Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
 and 572); groups of landowners impacted by a single link, such as the Lampasas J11

Landowners (who recommend Route 894, or similar alternatives that avoid Link J11);

groups of landowners impacted by multiple links, such as the Underwood Parties

(approximately 35 landowners, who oppose Links G41, G42, G43, G44, G45, and F8,

and support Route 894) and the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners (“27

landowners in Menard and Mason Counties who own over 10,000 acres of the 15,639

acres that would be directly impacted by Links M31, M32, and M33”); 1 and, in a recent

development, even comprise former pro se intervenors joining a pre-existing landowner

group after the hearing on the merits (e.g., the Moseley Group, which supports Route

894 or Route 487). But after the filing of initial briefs, the record still makes clear that

Route 894 is the route that best meets the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c) and PUC

SUBST. R. § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

II.    REPLY ARGUMENTS.

       E.     Route

              8.      Weighing the Factors in PURA § 37.056(c) and PUC Subst. R. §
                      25.101(b)(3)(B), which proposed transmission-line route is the
                      best alternative?

       A common theme found throughout the initial briefs is that no route is “perfect” or

that no route is “without flaws.” Nevertheless, when Route 894 is compared against

alternative routes intervenors impacted by Route 894 or Route 487 support (including a

“biased” route developed by impacted intervenors, Route CCG, not described in the

Application), 2 a holistic analysis of the data in the record confirms Route 894 is the route

the ALJs should recommend to the Commission.


1
       M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners’ Init. Br. at 4.
2
        5TR 269:19-270:12 (Anderson)(RFI routes “all reflect the bias of their single sole expert
or the landowner themselves”). Importantly, the Joint Applicants provided no notice of Route
CCG (or “Cherokee G” in the Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Initial Brief) pursuant to PUC
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                       2
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
           •   Route 296. The few parties who champion Route 296 emphasize that it

              parallels more compatible rights-of-way and property boundaries than

              Route 894 (47.07% vs. 43.92%). 3 But as the Combined Data Tables

              establish, that is the only primary data point in Route 296’s favor. 4 Not

              recognizing the statistical realities, some parties, such as Jerome and

              Gaylynn Sneed, allege that Route 296 “consistently outperform[s]” Route

              894. 5 Both the quantitative and qualitative metrics belie such a claim.

                  o Route 894 is cheaper.

                  o Route 894 directly affects 20 fewer habitable structures within 500

                     feet of the centerline.

                  o Route 894 does not impact any elementary schools or churches

                     among its 85 habitable structures. 6

                  o Route 894 crosses fewer streams.

                  o Route 894 has no estimated length of right-of-way within the

                     foreground visual zone of park/recreational areas.

                  o Route 894 crosses fewer cultural resource sites.



PROC. R. § 22.52. See 3TR. 47:19-24, 49:15-18 (Perkins) (“Q. . . . I’m just asking you whether
you sent out PUC Rule 22.52 notice to persons affected by the RFI routes after they were
devised? A. (Perkins) Not after they were devised.”).
3
       K13/K51 Landowners’ Init. Br. at 47-48.
4
          Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23, Combined Data Tables (derived of Oncor & LCRA TSC Exs.
1 and 1A, Application and Errata, Tables 7-1 (Route Composition), 7-2 (Environmental Data),
Attachment 4 (Estimated Costs)). Route 296 is longer, is more costly, affects more habitable
structures (including two churches and a Florence ISD elementary school), has more park
visibility, crosses far more streams, and more, than Route 894. Id.
5
       Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed Init. Br. at 2.
6
       Route 296, comprised in part of Link F34, does, in fact, directly impact both a Florence
ISD elementary school and two churches among its 105 recorded habitable structures. See
FISD Exhibit 1 (Direct Testimony); Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1A (Errata); Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex.
23 (Combined Data Tables).
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                     3
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
                   o Route 894 does not cross scientifically identified golden-cheeked

                       warbler habitat 7 or a habitat mitigation bank. 8

          •   Route 572. Unlike Route 296, Route 572 affects its 107 habitable

              structures even without utilizing Link F34. It does not impact an

              elementary school and churches like Route 296, but the Combined Data

              Tables and the record demonstrate that Route 572 offers no quantitative

              advantages over Route 894.

                  o Route 894 is more than two miles shorter, yet parallels almost four

                       more    miles   of   compatible       rights-of-way,   thereby   providing

                       substantially better paralleling. 9

                  o Route 894 is cheaper.

                  o Route 894 directly affects 22 fewer habitable structures within 500

                       feet of the centerline.

                  o Route 894 crosses significantly fewer streams (336, as compared

                       to 291).

                  o Route 894 not only crosses fewer cultural resource sites, but it also

                       crosses nearly 10 fewer miles of potential areas of high

                       archeological and historical sites.

                  o Route 894 does not cross scientifically identified golden-cheeked

                       warbler habitat or a habitat mitigation bank. 10


7

warblers in the path of Link J31).
8

through land designated as Golden-Cheeked Warbler mitigation acreage.”)
9
       See Hodge/Schwertner Ex. 1, Ex. BCA-3.
10
       See fn. 7, 8.
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                        4
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
            •   Route “CCG” or “Cherokee G”. Like Route 572, Route CCG also does not

               utilize Link F34, but the Combined Data Tables and the record yet again

               highlight another route that pales in comparison to Route 894.

                   o Route 894 is substantially cheaper (almost $74,000,000). 11

                   o Route 894 is almost 10 miles shorter.

                   o Route 894 directly affects 20 fewer habitable structures within 500

                      feet of the centerline.

                   o Route 894 crosses significantly fewer streams (346, as compared

                      to 291).

                   o Route 894 not only crosses fewer cultural resource sites, but it also

                      crosses almost eight fewer miles of potential areas of high

                      archeological and historical sites.

                   o Route 894 does not cross identified golden-cheeked warbler habitat

                      or a habitat mitigation bank. 12

       Because the numbers speak for themselves, the few opponents of Route 894 are

left to overstate certain qualitative reasons to avoid links on Route 894 or to use certain

links on other alternative routes. Alleged potential impacts upon Ecologically Significant

11
         Importantly, Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenor witness Reinecke completely disregards
cost in making her recommendation of Route CCG. CCP Ex. 1 (Reinecke Dir.)(mentioning the
cost factor in the framework, but expressly declining to address it in any way). While cost is not
the only—or often, even the primary—factor driving a routing decision, here, the difference in
costs between Route 894 and Route CCG is substantial. Yet Reinecke disregarded it
explicitly. CCP Ex. 2 28:13-18 (Reinecke Cross-reb.).
12
         The only “observations” of impacts on golden-cheeked warbler habitat made the basis of
Cherokee Creek, et al.’s, Save the Lampasas’s, and other testimony are theoretical, anecdotal,
or unsupported by scientific studies, other than those described in the Environmental
Assessment, which confirms that the contractors did no independent, onsite work—and made
no independent observations. See, e.g., Cherokee Creek Init. Br. at 32-33, Save the Lampasas
Init. Br. at 26-27. This contrasts to the evidence of two expert witnesses to the impact of a route
utilizing Link J31, such as Route CCG, upon a studied population and habitat mitigation bank.
See Ex. CRAI-5 (Morrison Dir.)(J31 impacts habitat and studied population of golden-cheeked
warblers); Underwood Ex. 34 (Blair Dir.)(J31 impacts golden-cheeked warbler mitigation bank).
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                         5
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
 Stream Segments (“ESSS”) is one example. As Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors

contend in their initial brief, “Route CCG avoids the ESSS-designated portion of the

Colorado River, which Route 894 and Route 487 do not.” 13 However, that group’s own

expert, Ms. Reinecke, testified to the contrary and acknowledged that Route 894 also

avoids the ESSS portion of the Colorado River. 14 In the same vein, the Cherokee Creek

group also argued that its preferred Route CCG “avoids USFWS Karst Zone 1 and the

Edwards Aquifer.” 15 But just like its ESSS claim, Cherokee Creek’s expert was forced to

concede that Route 894 also avoids both the Karst Zone and Edwards Aquifer. 16

       The Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors brief was not unique in making

inapposite comparisons. Other parties objecting to Route 894 embellished the

differences in routes, including the Colorado River crossings. Save the Lampasas, for

instance, asserts that Link J31 should be used, “as it parallels an existing compatible

corridor.” 17 However, the record undermines the notion of that specific crossing being

“compatible.” Even to the extent that Link J31 is “in the vicinity”18 of a pipeline corridor

for a short distance, as Commission Staff acknowledged, one of the reasons Link J31 is

“problematic,” and therefore not compatible, is because of the presence of petroleum

pipelines in the area. 19 It is clear from the maps that Link J31 is not routed in such a

manner that its proximity to a pipeline or any other corridor makes it less




13
       Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors’ Init. Br. at 30.
14
       5TR 222:2-6 (Reinecke).
15
       Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors’ Init. Br. at 36.
16
       5TR 221:21-222:1 (Reinecke).
17

18

19

 environmentally harmful—rather, it would be more so by fragmenting identified,

occupied golden-cheeked warbler habitat. 20

       Save the Lampasas both challenges the methodology of the Environmental

Assessment and argues that routes utilizing river crossings that affect them are too

close to state parks. 21 The K13/K51 Landowners argue similarly. 22



20
       See Ex. CRAI-11 (showing distances of Link J31 from pipeline corridor); Ex. CRAI-5
13:4-14:9, 20:11-24:14 (Morrison Dir.).
21
         For instance, Save the Lampasas criticizes reliance upon Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, 1A,
23 data as set forth in Table 7-3, because it draws a “binary designation” for impacts upon
parks. Save the Lampasas Init. Br. at 16. But to make a larger point illustrated here, many
statistics in the Environmental Assessment are chosen with an eye to line-drawing, e.g.,
proximity to habitable structures (500 feet); distances from existing rights-of-way that count for
paralleling purposes vs. those that are too far away; and yes, distances from parks.
Certain parties compound this problem by criticizing the statistical counts, such as right-of-way
paralleling, applied to specific links, claiming “double counting,” or that their impacted links have
additional structures “just beyond the 520 feet benchmark” See, e.g., Save the Lampasas Init.
Br. at 32-35, G-9 and G-13 Landowners’ Init. Br., at 9. These parties fail to recognize that the
Joint Applicants’ routing methodology, including “bisections” or other impacts on individual
landowners, however flawed, was applied Study Area-wide and impacts all tracts in similar
ways.
Simply reviewing the testimony in the record and Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 21 (Intervenor
Map), it is apparent that most party-landowners are “bisected,” not passed near a
property line or along other compatible rights-of-way. Parties’ claims that they are uniquely
affected by failures to parallel are not supported in the record. Id. As Staff witness Poole
testified:
       Q. . . . And you have seen the testimony submitted by hundreds of intervenors in this
       matter, and it seems like a great number of those intervenors state that the proposed
       links bisect their properties rather than paralleling property. Is that fair?
       A. Yes. I’ve seen that.
4TR.20-25 (Poole).
Certainly, no party to this case wants the transmission line built on its land, and certainly,
impacts on individuals and communities matter, but the task before the Commission is to
choose the best route, which will inevitably have localized negative impacts on the landowners
and communities affected by the chosen route. Those localized impacts, while valuable in the
balancing analysis before the ALJs and the Commission, may not overshadow the end-to-end
route-evaluation balancing process the law requires. See Dunn v. Public Utility Commission of
Texas, 246 S.W.3d 788, 795 (Tex. App.—Austin 2008, no pet.). However flawed the Joint
Applicants’ experts’ methodologies may have been in preparing the Environmental Assessment
and list of proposed routes, there is no evidence that the types of problems identified with some
links do not apply Study Area wide.
22
       K13/K51 Landowners’ Init. Br. at 9-25.
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                           7
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
        Specifically, Save the Lampasas argues that Link J31 should be used for

crossing the Colorado River because of its distance from certain state parks. 23

However, in doing so, Save the Lampasas mischaracterizes Mr. Poole’s testimony and

misstates the distance of Link J22 (used in Route 894) from the parks. 24 Mr. Poole

never testified that Link J22 sits “within half a mile of these parks” and the record, as

well as briefing from other parties, confirms that it does not. 25

       Critically, the K13/K51 Landowners multi-page argument on this subject is also

marked by overstatements and cherry-picked support. The most egregious example is

its claim that “The J31 crossing is the best-supported Colorado River crossing in the

record.” 26 To the contrary, as Staten Creek Ranch effectively argued in its initial brief,

when looking at the crossings in isolation (which the ALJs should not do), Link U3, of all

the Colorado River crossings, is the one best supported by the record. Although the

K13/K51 landowners support the use of Link U3 in Routes 410 and 392 if a northern

route is ultimately selected, they curiously ignored Link U3 when comparing Colorado

River crossings. 27 As Staten Creek Ranch reasoned, Link U3 is the farthest from the

state parks, thereby nullifying any viewshed argument, and Link U3 is “already

disturbed” by a transmission line crossing the Colorado River at that point. 28 The

K13/K51 Landowners not only evaluated a single-link in isolation, they didn’t even

evaluate all available options, including one that performs best.


23
       Save the Lampasas’ Init. Br. at 37.
24
       Id.
25
       See Ex. CRAI-11 (showing distances from park); see also Staten Creek Ranch’s Init. Br.
at 7; 4TR 116:5-7 (Poole)(Q. Roughly, you know, half a mile to a mile from those parks? A.
Yeah. I wouldn't dispute that.)
26
       Id. at 28.
27
       Id. at 55; Id. at 25-28 (comparing Links J11, J22, J26, and J31).
28
       Staten Creek Ranch’s Init. Br. at 31-33.
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349; PUC Docket No. 59475                                   8
Colorado River Alliance Intervenors’ Reply Brief
        A flawed single-link analysis of the Colorado River crossings does not support

Routes 296, 572, and CCG, or using Link J31, and what is more, under a proper route-

wide evaluation, other criteria such as environmental integrity further demonstrate that

Routes 296, 572, and CCG are not better alternatives to Route 894. Notably, none of

the initial briefs of the proponents of Routes 296, 572, and CCG challenged Dr. Michael

Morrison or Ms. Jennifer Blair’s contentions that a route comprised in part of Link J31

would directly impact identified and occupied—not merely theorized or modeled—

endangered species habitat of the golden-cheeked warbler on Link J31. While some

parties discuss impacts upon golden-cheeked warbler habitat projected under the

Mueller model, the uncontroverted evidence in this record confirms that any route

comprised in part of Link J31 would fragment known, occupied golden-cheeked warbler

habitat and a habitat mitigation bank. 29

III.   CONCLUSION.

       For all of the reasons proven in the record and set forth in its initial and reply

brief, Colorado Rivers Alliance Intervenors respectfully request that the ALJs

recommend and the Commission select Route 894.

impacts on individuals and communities matter, but the task before the Commission is to
choose the best route, which will inevitably have localized negative impacts on the landowners

balancing analysis before the ALJs and the Commission, may not overshadow the end-to-end
route - evaluation balancing process the law requires . See Dunn v. Public Utility Commission of
Texas, 246 S.W.3d 788, 795 (Tex. App.-Austin 2008, no pet.). However flawed the Joint
Applicants' experts' methodologies may have been in preparing the Environmental Assessment
and list of proposed routes, there is no evidence that the types of problems identified with some
